newsitem.title: CANADA: B.C. lumber officials hope for labor deal by July.
newsitem.headline: B.C. lumber officials hope for labor deal by July.

text.p: Negotiators for British Columbia's coastal forestry companies and the lumber workers union said on Wednesday they did not expect a deal on a new labor contract before the current accord expires on June 14.
Dave Haggard, president of the IWA-Canada union, said in an interview that the next several weeks would be crucial.
"I wouldn't be that optimistic (to expect an agreement by June 14), but I hope by July we are very, very close to an agreement," he said.

"Otherwise we will have to seriously evaluate what we are going to do -- take a strike vote or whatever. My intent is to get as close to a collective agreement (as possible) before July," Haggard said.
Keith Bennett, chief negotiator for the 65 companies that bargain as the Forest Industrial Relations group, also called it "unrealistic" to expect a deal before June 14.
But he said he hoped for an agreement "soon thereafter... (in) July hopefully."

The two sides began negotiations in earnest today after earlier preliminary meetings to exchange agendas. They both predicted difficult negotiations ahead and said they would meet continuously for at least three weeks.
The contract agreed upon by companies on the British Columbia coast is used as a benchmark for other areas of the province. The lumber sector employs about 29,000 workers in the province.

The union's main demands are for enhanced job security, a reduction in time worked with no decrease in pay and increased benefits. "The thing we're looking at is getting more people to work in our industry," Haggard said.
Bennett said his financially strapped member companies were unable to bear the increase in costs that would result from limits on overtime and a shortening of the work week.
He criticized British Columbia Premier Glen Clark for supporting ideas such as a shorter work week and an overtime cap. Bennett declined to say what the companies' highest priority issue would be.

Separately, British Columbia is negotiating with forest companies in an effort to strike a deal that would increase jobs in the forest sector by 21,000 by 2001 in exchange for relief from regulatory costs and a streamlining of bureaucracy.
